analysis.answer: Current law allows demonstrations on public sidewalks subject to general traffic and noise rules. The proposed measure specifically prohibits demonstrating within 100 feet of the entrance to any facility that provides abortion services during its operating hours.

Patients and staff of abortion facilities benefit from reduced confrontation and unimpeded physical access to the entrances. Demonstrators bear the cost of having their ability to express themselves restricted in those specific locations.

Demonstrators will likely move their activities to just outside the 100-foot boundary. Law enforcement will need to measure and enforce this specific distance. Patients and staff may face fewer direct interactions with protesters immediately at the facility doors.

The measure addresses the problem of confrontation, obstruction, or harassment at the immediate entrances of abortion clinics. The mechanism of a 100-foot buffer zone removes demonstrators from the immediate vicinity, reducing physical barriers to entry, but it also restricts speech and expression in those public spaces.
Law enforcement agencies gain the power and discretion to determine what activities qualify as demonstrating and to enforce the 100-foot boundary around facility entrances.

Researchers and legal experts disagree on the effects of buffer zones. Some findings emphasize that buffer zones effectively protect patient access and reduce violence or harassment at clinics, while others argue they primarily chill protected First Amendment speech and prevent peaceful counseling.

flags.note: The term is not defined, leaving it ambiguous whether it applies to silent prayer, holding signs, or distributing literature.
The phrase is not defined and could expansively include large general hospitals, potentially restricting demonstrations on unrelated issues near their entrances.
